title: Reading evidence about a parenting programme
instructions: Read the five-paragraph text. Match paragraphs A–E to the same shared list of headings A–H; use a heading at most once. Answer the remaining view and summary questions. This is a shorter preparatory set, not a full IELTS Reading section.

stimulus.text:
A. A historical report describes Leeds recording a fall in childhood obesity, with the clearest change among families in the most disadvantaged areas. It compares that pattern with improvement in Amsterdam, another city where the problem had proved difficult to address. The contrast matters because a city-wide average can conceal different experiences among groups. In the Leeds account, the improvement among poorer children attracted particular attention, rather than being treated as an incidental detail beneath one overall number. These are findings described in that report, not a claim about present-day rates.

B. Researchers examined several years of measurements rather than one isolated result. A national programme measured children at the beginning and end of primary school, and comparable places offered a background against which to consider Leeds. However, the researcher did not claim certainty about the reason for the decline. A programme called Henry, introduced as part of the city’s strategy, was a possible contributor. The evidence could support interest in that programme without establishing that it alone caused the observed change. Repeated observations and a confident causal explanation are different forms of claim.

C. Henry’s approach was described as authoritative rather than authoritarian. Parents retained responsibility and set limits, while responding to their children and offering bounded choices. This differed both from imposing every decision and from allowing children unrestricted freedom. A child might choose between two vegetables rather than decide whether there would be any vegetables. A bedtime choice could concern where a story would be read. These examples illustrate a relationship between clear boundaries and participation, rather than a simple instruction to refuse every request a child makes.

D. A parent who attended the programme described learning about healthy eating and saving money through planning meals. She also reported benefits beyond food. Sharing ideas with her partner helped the family, and she associated the approach with calmer, happier children and lower stress for the adults. Her account conveys why participation felt worthwhile to her. It remains an individual’s experience, however, rather than a separate statistical measurement of outcomes for every participating household. The different types of evidence can be read together without being mistaken for each other.

E. The local public-health perspective emphasised helping families early, before an established problem became harder to tackle. It also recognised that parents know their own circumstances and what changes they can realistically make. The aim was to work alongside them, rather than assume that one solution fitted everyone. A national minister welcomed local work that made healthy choices easier for busy parents. Taken together, these comments frame practical support and prevention as important aims, while leaving room for the uncertainty about causation already acknowledged by the researcher.

criteria.label: Textual evidence
criteria.description: Use only the stated text, respect scope and word limits, and distinguish contradiction from insufficient information.

answerKey.rationale: The whole of paragraph A develops: An improvement especially visible in disadvantaged groups. Read its central relationship and qualification, not an isolated repeated word.
The whole of paragraph B develops: Separating a repeated pattern from a certain cause. Read its central relationship and qualification, not an isolated repeated word.
The whole of paragraph C develops: Combining parental limits with children’s choices. Read its central relationship and qualification, not an isolated repeated word.
The whole of paragraph D develops: A participant’s account of benefits across family life. Read its central relationship and qualification, not an isolated repeated word.
The whole of paragraph E develops: Supporting realistic early changes in families. Read its central relationship and qualification, not an isolated repeated word.
B distinguishes repeated observations from certainty about a single cause.

assessment.feedbackGuidance: After submission, state each paragraph’s main claim before discussing the heading. Identify a distractor that repeats the subject but changes the relationship or scope. In the city teaching example, northern location is introductory while unusual regulation is the paragraph’s focus; a topic word is not the whole argument. For YES/NO/NOT GIVEN use the writer’s actual position, and distinguish uncertainty about cause from denial of an observed change. For summary completion copy one exact word with grammatical fit. Revise one gist statement and explain one rejected qualifier. Raw accuracy only; no band.
